Action Plan:
1. Left-sided hearing loss: Arrange face-to-face otoscopic ear examination within 4–5 days at a clinic so a GP can inspect the left ear drum and canal; if impacted cerumen is found, perform safe ear wax removal in clinic. Admin team to be notified to slot patient into clinic; patient instructed to call support team number in notes to confirm booking. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.
2. Left-sided tinnitus: Provide patient with an educational leaflet about tinnitus (link to be pasted into appointment notes); ask patient to read leaflet before clinic visit and document understanding. Reassess tinnitus after ear exam to decide on further management (e.g., audiometry, ENT referral, symptomatic measures) if ear is clear.
3. Intermittent dizziness/lightheadedness with mild nausea: Assess vestibular symptoms at the clinic visit alongside ear exam. If otoscopy is normal or symptoms persist/worsen, arrange audiometry and consider ENT referral; if indicated by audiometry or persistent unilateral sensorineural loss, consider MRI/internal acoustic meatus imaging to evaluate for retrocochlear causes. Advise patient to seek urgent care if dizziness becomes severe, rotational vertigo occurs, or new neurological symptoms develop.
4. Ear-care advice: Advise patient to stop inserting cotton buds into ears (documented in notes). Provide guidance on avoiding self-ear cleaning and follow-up plan.
5. Follow-up and escalation: If issues develop between now and clinic appointment, patient to rebook a video appointment or seek urgent assessment. Documented plan and instructions left in notes for covering GP.
6. Documentation: Clinician will paste tinnitus leaflet link and support team contact in the appointment notes.

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: Deterioration of hearing in left ear for ~6 weeks; patient reports left-sided ringing (tinnitus) and occasional mild dizziness with some nausea.
- Onset/duration: Symptoms started ~6 weeks ago; prior brief episode ~1 year ago lasting a couple of days.
- Symptom characteristics:
  - Hearing difficulty: unilateral (left), intermittent, described as muffled.
  - Tinnitus: intermittent, left-sided; masked/relieved by external sound (watching TV/listening to music).
  - Dizziness: mild, not true spinning/vertigo; occasional lightheadedness and slight nausea.
  - No reported ear pain, no ear discharge, no fever.
- Ear-care behavior: Patient admits to using cotton buds (doctor advised against this).
- Past medical history: Not reported / not documented in transcript.
- Previous surgeries: Not reported.
- Medications: Not reported / not documented.
- Allergies: Not reported / not documented.
- Social history / family history: Not reported / not documented.

Objective:
- No vital signs recorded in transcript.
- No physical examination findings recorded; planned: in-person otoscopic examination of the left ear to assess for cerumen impaction or tympanic membrane pathology.
- No investigations/results recorded during this encounter.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Left-sided hearing loss:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Cerumen (earwax) impaction / conductive hearing loss. (DDx: "Cerumen (earwax) impaction / obstructive conductive hearing loss" — Likelihood: High)
   - Differential diagnosis (consistent with DDx):
     - Vestibular schwannoma (DDx item: Vestibular schwannoma / acoustic neuroma — Likelihood: Medium) — supports unilateral progressive hearing loss + tinnitus + imbalance.
     - Viral cochleitis / labyrinthitis (DDx item: Otitis media / externa or viral cochleitis/labyrinthitis — Likelihood: Medium) — supports unilateral hearing change with tinnitus and dizziness.
     - Meniere disease / endolymphatic hydrops (DDx item: Meniere disease — Likelihood: Low to Medium) — less likely given dizziness not classic vertigo.
     - Noise-induced or idiopathic sensorineural hearing loss (DDx item: Noise-induced or sensorineural hearing loss) — possible if sensorineural pattern found.
   - Investigations planned:
     - Immediate: Face-to-face otoscopic ear examination within 4–5 days (to assess for cerumen impaction or visible middle/inner ear pathology).
     - If otoscopy normal or hearing loss persists: Pure-tone audiometry and tympanometry as next steps (recommended / to be arranged).
     - If audiometry shows asymmetric sensorineural loss: consider MRI with attention to internal acoustic meatus (retrocochlear imaging) — per DDx concern for vestibular schwannoma (Medium).
   - Treatment planned:
     - If cerumen impaction identified: in-clinic ear wax removal (microsuction or irrigation as appropriate).
     - No medications documented or prescribed at this visit.
   - Referrals:
     - ENT referral and audiology referral if otoscopy is normal and hearing loss persists or if audiometry shows sensorineural asymmetry.

2. Tinnitus (left-sided):
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Tinnitus (symptom). (Supported DDx items: Cerumen impaction — High; Vestibular schwannoma — Medium; Viral cochleitis — Medium; Meniere disease — Low to Medium)
   - Differential diagnosis (consistent with DDx):
     - Conductive cause from cerumen impaction (High).
     - Sensorineural causes including vestibular schwannoma (Medium), viral cochleitis (Medium), Meniere disease (Low–Medium).
   - Investigations planned:
     - Reassess after otoscopic exam; arrange audiometry if ear is clear or tinnitus persists.
   - Treatment planned:
     - Provide educational leaflet about tinnitus (link to be placed in notes); patient to read prior to clinic.
     - Symptomatic management to be discussed after assessment (not specified at this visit).
   - Referrals:
     - Audiology and/or ENT if tinnitus persists or if audiometry demonstrates abnormal findings.

3. Intermittent dizziness / lightheadedness with nausea:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Vestibular schwannoma (DDx item: Vestibular schwannoma / acoustic neuroma — Likelihood: Medium). (Note: transcript clinician considered possible balance-system involvement; DDx lists vestibular schwannoma and other vestibular causes.)
   - Differential diagnosis (consistent with DDx):
     - Viral cochleitis / labyrinthitis (Medium) — can cause dizziness and hearing change.
     - Meniere disease (Low–Medium) — typically causes discrete severe vertigo episodes, less consistent with mild symptoms.
     - Vertebrobasilar insufficiency / posterior circulation ischemia (DDx Vindicate list) — possible cause of combined auditory and vestibular symptoms; less likely given subacute, intermittent mild symptoms and absence of other brainstem signs.
     - Ototoxicity or other metabolic causes — less likely without medication/exposure history (medications not documented).
   - Investigations planned:
     - Evaluate vestibular symptoms during clinic visit; consider audiometry and ENT assessment if symptoms persist.
     - Consider neuroradiological imaging (MRI internal acoustic meatus/brain) if audiometry or clinical findings suggest retrocochlear pathology (e.g., asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss) or if symptoms progress.
   - Treatment planned:
     - Symptomatic advice at clinic as needed; urgent escalation if symptoms worsen (severe vertigo, new neurological signs).
   - Referrals:
     - ENT and audiology if persistent or if investigation indicates sensorineural/retrocochlear cause.
     - Urgent medical assessment if new/worsening neurological symptoms.
